transcript.text: Shark NV602UK has lost loads of suction and whistles. Found a split in the flexible hose near the handle end. Is it the hose I need?

Quite possibly, yes. A split in the flexible hose is a classic cause of exactly this: air gets sucked in through the gap instead of through the floorhead, so pickup drops sharply, and the air rushing through a narrow split often makes a whistle. A split near the handle end is common too, because that's where the hose flexes most. Before you commit to a new hose, it's worth confirming the split is the whole story. A weak hose often fails because something else is choking the airflow, and lost suction usually has more than one contributor. Do these with the vacuum unplugged: 1. Tape the split as a test. Wrap it tightly with a few turns of duct tape or electrical tape, then plug in and try it. If the whistle stops and the suction comes back strongly, the hose is your fault. Tape is only a stopgap, as it won't last on a part that flexes. If the suction is still weak, something else is also wrong.
2. Check for blockages. Detach the hose and wand and look through each one, or drop a coin through. It should fall straight out. Also check the neck of the floorhead and the inlet into the dust bin. A partial blockage can make its own whistle and puts extra strain on the hose.
3. Empty the bin and wash the filters. Wash them in cold water only and let them dry fully for at least 24 hours before refitting them. Clogged filters are the most common cause of suction slowly fading. If taping the split brings the suction back, a replacement flexible hose is the fix. These are usually an owner-fit part on uprights like this. If it's still weak after the tape, the blockage and filter checks will tell us where to look next. Let me know how the tape test goes.

Already tried covering the split with my hand while it's running and suction comes back much better, and I've taped it for now. Hose is clear and I cleaned the filters last week with little change. So do I just need a new hose, or the hose and handle together?

Covering the split brought the suction back strongly and the hose is clear, so the split is probably your main fault. I'm fairly sure of that. Whether you need just the hose or the hose and handle together depends on how the two are joined and where the damage is. On many Shark uprights the flexible hose is a separate part that clips or twists into the handle, but on some versions it comes fixed to the handle as one assembly. 1. Look at where the hose meets the handle. If there's a release clip, a collar that twists, or a couple of screws, the hose usually comes away on its own. A hose-only replacement is then normally enough.
2. Check where exactly the split is. If it's in the ribbed hose, even close to the end, the handle is fine. 3. Check whether the hose is fixed permanently into the handle with no way to separate them. If so, it's sold as one piece and you'd be replacing both anyway. When you search for the part, use the full model number from the rating label. Check that the listing says it fits that model and shows the same end fittings as yours. One more check while it's taped: is the suction fully back to how it used to be, or just much better? If it's still a bit down, turn the floorhead over and clear any hair round the brush bar. Also check the floorhead neck and the bin inlet, because a hose usually splits at a flex point but can be helped along by extra strain. If it's back to normal, the hose is the whole story.

The split is in the ribbed hose just by the handle cuff, so the handle itself looks fine. I'm not sure if the hose comes off the handle separately though. Suction with the tape on is much better but I haven't checked if it's fully back to normal.

With the split in the ribbed section and the handle undamaged, the flexible hose is probably the part at fault. Covering the split brought the suction back, and the hose is otherwise clear. I'm confident in that. You shouldn't need a new handle. Whether the hose comes on its own or with end fittings depends on how yours is put together. Replacement hoses are commonly sold as a hose assembly with both end cuffs already fitted, rather than as bare tubing. 1. Unplug it and look closely at the cuff where the hose meets the handle. A release button, a latch, a collar that twists or a couple of small screws means the hose detaches separately. That's normally a hose-only job.
2. Do the same at the other end, where the hose joins the main body. A hose assembly needs to come free at both ends.
3. If the cuff looks moulded permanently into the handle with no fixing at all, the hose and handle are likely supplied as one piece. In that case the handle would come with it, even though yours is fine. When you look at parts listings, search by the full model number from the rating label. One quick check is worth doing. Unplug it, turn the floorhead over and look for hair or thread round the brush bar, then make sure the bar spins freely by hand. Also look into the floorhead neck. If it's clean, the hose is the whole story and the new one should bring it back to normal. If it's tangled, clearing it will give you back the last bit of pickup too.
Thanks. I'm still not sure if the hose comes off the handle separately. Is there a way to tell which one to buy, or should I just get the hose and handle together to be safe?

Yes, there are a few reliable ways to tell, and they're better than buying the hose and handle together just in case. That combined part usually costs a fair bit more, and it may not even be how the parts are supplied for your model. 1. Compare photos. Find listings using the full model number from the rating label. Look closely at the photos of the hose-only part. If the cuff at the handle end looks like a plain fitting that pushes or latches in, compare it with your own handle joint. A matching shape usually means a separate hose will fit.
2. Check the manual or parts diagram. The user manual or the exploded parts diagram on parts sites often shows the hose as its own item. If it's listed separately for your model number, it comes off separately.
3. Ask Shark. Their customer service can confirm from the model and serial number which part covers a split in the ribbed hose near the handle cuff. That's the surest route if the photos leave you unsure.
4. Look at the joint itself. With it unplugged, check the handle cuff for a release button or catch, a twist collar or small screws. If you find one, the hose comes away separately. If it's genuinely moulded in with nothing to undo, it's likely a one-piece assembly. Whichever it turns out to be, the hose is very likely the part at fault. Your handle looks fine, so you only need the combined assembly if the hose can't be bought on its own. If the bar was clean and spun freely, the hose should be the whole story. How did it look?
I haven't looked at the brush bar yet. I'll check the handle joint for a catch or screws and compare photos with the NV602UK listings. If I can't tell, I'll ask Shark. Thanks.

That sounds like a sensible plan. A catch, twist collar or screws at the handle cuff, or a matching cuff shape in the hose-only photos, will usually settle it. Shark can confirm it from the serial number if you're still unsure. The split hose is very likely the main cause. Covering it brought the suction back and the hose is otherwise clear. The handle looks fine, so you'd only need the combined assembly if the hose isn't supplied on its own. While you're checking the joint, it's worth doing the brush bar check too. 1. Unplug the vacuum and turn the floorhead over.
2. Cut away any hair or thread wrapped round the brush bar and at the end caps.
3. Spin the bar by hand. It should turn freely.
4. Look into the floorhead neck for anything lodged there. If it's clean and turns freely, the hose is the whole story. If it's tangled, clearing it will bring back the last bit of pickup that the tape alone may not. Expect it to loosen with use, though, because that part of the hose flexes a lot. Let me know what you find at the joint or the brush bar if anything doesn't add up.
